title: TP-Link problems in US grow amid FCC router ban and four state lawsuits
gist: Four Republican-led states (Florida, Montana, Iowa, Nebraska) sued TP-Link alleging it lied about its China ties and router security, while the FCC's six-month-old ban on foreign-made consumer routers still has no exemption for TP-Link despite exemptions for Netgear, Asus, Amazon Eero, Starlink and others. TP-Link says the suits are built on false premises and that its devices are made in Vietnam by an independent US company.

insights.claim: Florida, Montana, Iowa and Nebraska, all with Republican attorneys general, sued TP-Link alleging unfair and deceptive trade practices under state consumer protection laws for misleading consumers about router safety and China ties.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Coordinated state action adds legal and reputational risk on top of the federal ban.
insights.locator: TP-Link is facing more legal troubles

insights.claim: Florida AG James Uthmeier calls TP-Link's claim of splitting from China and manufacturing in Vietnam 'fiction', saying research and manufacturing remain rooted in China, and seeks an injunction, restitution and penalties.
insights.speaker: James Uthmeier
insights.so_what: States are contesting TP-Link's origin story, the core of its US defense.
insights.locator: Florida AG says TP-Link defense is “fiction”

insights.claim: The suits cite an April 2025 Bloomberg report that, aside from components bought in Vietnam accounting for 0.5 percent of input value at the plant, all other components are imported from China.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Final assembly in Vietnam may not satisfy a regulator's 'non-Chinese' test if component sourcing is overwhelmingly Chinese.
insights.locator: The lawsuit cites an April 2025 Bloomberg article

insights.claim: The lawsuits note US officials weighed banning TP-Link routers as an 'unacceptable risk' and point to Russian GRU exploitation of TP-Link vulnerabilities and use of a Chinese construction contractor for the Vietnam plant expansion.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Security allegations are being tied to consumer-deception law as a legal route to restrict sales.
insights.locator: The lawsuits note that even before the FCC

insights.claim: TP-Link calls the coordinated lawsuits 'built on false premises', says its devices are manufactured in Vietnam and that TP-Link Systems is an independent US company not controlled by any foreign government, and says it will not share customer network data with foreign governments.
insights.speaker: Steve Kovsky
insights.so_what: TP-Link's rebuttal rests on corporate independence and manufacturing location documentation.
insights.quote: “The coordinated lawsuits are built on false premises,”

themes.theme: FCC foreign router ban and exemptions

insights.claim: The FCC announced about six months ago a sweeping ban on consumer routers made wholly or partly outside the US, and exemptions have gone to Netgear, Asus, Adtran, Amazon/Eero, Calix, Nokia, SpaceX's Starlink and others, but not TP-Link.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Competitors with exemptions gain relative position in the US router market while TP-Link is singled out.

insights.claim: TP-Link cannot sell its latest Wi-Fi 8 routers in the US, though models approved before the ban can still be sold.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The ban blocks TP-Link's next-gen product cycle in the US, creating a growing revenue and share gap.
insights.locator: For now, TP-Link is unable to sell

insights.claim: To get an exemption, makers need a DoD or DHS determination of no national security risk, a justification of why the router is not made in the US, and a time-bound US manufacturing plan.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The exemption path forces reshoring commitments, an industrial policy lever.
insights.locator: The FCC process requires each router maker

insights.claim: TP-Link told FCC Chairman Brendan Carr's staff in April that it is investing hundreds of millions of dollars to bring consumer router manufacturing and R&D to the US and already has over 550 US employees, but there has been little news on its application.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Reshoring pledges are TP-Link's route to an exemption, with no approval yet visible.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, there has been little news

insights.claim: TP-Link moved its headquarters to California in October 2024 amid investigations into attacks linked to the Chinese government, including a botnet composed mostly of TP-Link routers.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The HQ move did not insulate TP-Link from regulators, who focus on supply chain rather than domicile.
insights.locator: TP-Link was founded in China but moved

insights.claim: NCTA, the cable industry lobby, petitioned the FCC for a waiver letting ISPs swap components because of supply chain shortages, to prevent disruptions in broadband availability.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The ban is creating supply friction for US broadband providers upgrading customer equipment.
insights.locator: US-based broadband providers are also seeking changes
